newsitem.title: USA: Dole needs debate win, but will people watch?.
newsitem.headline: Dole needs debate win, but will people watch?.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
Republican Bob Dole is looking towards Sunday's campaign debate to cut President Bill Clinton's big lead, but he faces a daunting public perception that the campaign is already all but over.
One remarkable aspect of the 1996 presidential campaign is how stable it has been. Clinton's current lead of between 10 to 18 percentage points has barely changed since late Spring.
As a result, 79 percent of respondents in a poll by the Pew Research Centre this week said they expected Clinton to win on November 5.

But the view that the race is already over may lower the television audience for the two debates, the first of which takes place on Sunday. In the Pew poll, only 43 percent of voters said they were "very likely" to watch the debates, compared to 67 percent in 1992, when the final debate attracted an audience of 95 million.

Fewer than one third said the debates would matter to them in deciding whom to support. Of those who said they were very likely or somewhat likely to watch the debates, 48 percent said they had already made up their minds on their vote.

Television audiences for key events in this year's campaign have been consistently lower than in 1992. Only 12.1 million television sets were turned on for the first night of the Republican convention, down 20 percent from the same night four years ago. The first night audience for the Democratic convention was 21 percent lower than 1992.

"There simply hasn't been any pivotal issue or surprising revelation in this campaign since April," said David Birdsell, a political scientist with Baruch College in New York who has written a book about presidential debates.
Dole himself insists that voters have yet to start paying attention to the race.

"One of our surveys showed that only 27 percent of the American people are tuned into the presidential race and that there are a lot of people out there who have yet to take note of what's happening," he said.
But a Reuters poll on Friday found that attitudes had hardened and that, if anything, Dole's support was slightly softer than Clinton's.
Some 63 percent of Clinton backers said their support for the president was "very strong", 29 percent said it was "somewhat strong" and 7 percent said it was "not strong."
For Dole, the equivalent figures were: 60 percent very strong, 30 percent somewhat strong and 10 percent not strong.
The Reuters poll found that only about 12 percent of likely voters remain undecided -- the likeliest group to be swayed by the candidates' performances.
"If we assume that the debates have their greatest influence on undecided voters, they could be highly significant, but only if the race tightens," said Birdsell.

Past debates have gone down in U.S. political history as providing pivotal moments in presidential campaigns. But a study by the Annenberg School for Communication said their effects may have been overestimated.
"In 1992, as in other years, the debates had little effect on the electoral outcome," the study concluded.

Polls taken before and after the 1992 presidential debates found that almost 90 percent of voters stuck to their pre-debate choices. Even if voters thought the other man won, most did not change their minds.

Still, negative impressions forged during debates can stick to politicians for the rest of their lives. Dole's main challenge Sunday may be to correct his image for being "mean" and "harsh", first created in a vice presidentialial candidates debate with Democrat Walter Mondale 20 years ago.
"Dole must make a case against Clinton without sounding clipped and mean and without making over-sweeping claims," said Birdsell.
